eng-b1-field-notes-to-technical-report-d.walkthrough:
Dana is a structural EIT who just got back from a two-hour site visit inspecting a parking structure with a mix of slab cracking, an exposed rebar condition, and a drainage issue. Her notebook is full of shorthand: measurements, abbreviations, and a few things she flagged to look into further but didn't have time to fully assess on site.

Back at her desk, she opens Claude and pastes the lesson's prompt, filling in the report type (structural condition assessment), project name, site visit date, and her role. She then pastes her raw notes exactly as written: "NW corner, 2nd flr slab - hairline crack ~14ft run, max width 1/16in. Rebar exposed at col C4 base, approx 6in section, corrosion visible. Roof drain #3 - ponding, standing water 1/2in noted at 2pm, dry weather."

Claude returns a draft organized by location: Second Floor Northwest Corner, Column C4 Base, and Roof Drain #3, with exact measurements preserved - 14 ft crack run, 1/16 in max width, 6 in exposed section. At the corrosion note, it inserts "[CLARIFY: extent/depth of corrosion not specified in notes]" rather than rating severity, since Dana's notes never did. Recommendations is left as "[ENGINEER TO COMPLETE]."

Dana reads the draft against her notebook and photos. She notices the draft grouped two separate slab observations that were actually at different columns - a mixup from the notes being adjacent on the page. She sends a follow-up asking Claude to double check nothing was merged beyond her notes, and it separates the two observations correctly on the second pass.

She then writes her own professional recommendations - flagging the column for further investigation given the corrosion, and noting the drain needs cleaning and monitoring - fills in the clarify flag with her own assessment after re-examining her photos, and routes the completed report through her firm's standard senior engineer review before it goes final. Total time from opening her notebook to a review-ready draft: about 20 minutes, versus the hour or more it used to take to type up a report from scratch.

eng-b2-explain-technical-concepts-to-sta.walkthrough:
Marcus is a structural engineer on a residential addition project. Geotechnical testing came back showing a soft clay layer at six feet depth, which means the foundation needs to go deeper than originally planned - adding real cost the homeowner client wasn't expecting. He needs to explain this clearly without the client feeling blindsided or confused.

He opens ChatGPT and starts with his own accurate technical description, typed in his own words: "We're specifying a deeper foundation than the client expected because geotechnical testing found a soft clay layer at 6ft depth that won't support the standard footing design without excessive settlement over time." Audience: homeowner client. What they need to understand: why the foundation cost is higher than the original estimate, and he needs them to approve the additional cost.

ChatGPT returns a 200-word explanation: it describes the soft clay layer found in testing, explains that a standard foundation resting on it would slowly sink unevenly, cracking walls and floors, and uses an analogy about a table with an uneven leg needing a shim - noting the foundation itself is being changed so it never needs one. It includes a glossary for "settlement" and "geotechnical testing," and closes stating the client is being asked to approve the deeper foundation and its added cost.

Marcus reads it against his own description and the substance holds - nothing about the risk got dropped. But he's not sure the table-leg analogy is quite right, since it might imply a small patch rather than a structural change. He flags that concern, and ChatGPT revises the analogy to make clear the foundation is being redesigned, not just shimmed.

He reads the final version once more, confirms it matches his own understanding, and uses it as the basis for both an email to the client and what he says on their next call. The whole process took about 10 minutes, and the client approved the cost increase without a drawn-out back-and-forth, because the reasoning was clear from the first message.

eng-i1-review-checklists-for-documents-a.walkthrough:
Aisha is a project engineer at a mid-size structural firm who reviews steel connection submittals regularly, but has always done it from memory and a mental checklist that varies slightly depending on how busy she is. After catching a near-miss where a bolt grade mismatch almost slipped through, she decides to build a real, written checklist.

She opens Claude and fills in the lesson's prompt: discipline is structural, document type is a steel connection design submittal, governing code is AISC 360 and the locally adopted IBC edition, and her firm has no existing formal checklist for this yet, so she writes "NONE."

Claude returns a checklist under four categories: General/Coordination, Design Criteria, Details, and Code Compliance. Under General/Coordination, it asks whether connection loads match the framing drawings, and whether member sizes match the drawing set. Under Design Criteria, it tags the design-basis-edition item with [VERIFY CURRENT CODE/STANDARD], since it can't confirm her jurisdiction's adopted edition. Under Details, it asks whether bolt grade, size, and quantity are consistent between calc and detail - directly addressing the near-miss that prompted this exercise. Under Code Compliance, another verification flag appears on edge distance requirements.

Aisha reviews it and notices one item is phrased as a flat statement rather than a question - it reads "Bolt grade matches project standard" instead of asking her to check it. She sends a follow-up asking Claude to rewrite any item phrased as an assertion rather than a question, and the revised version fixes it to "Does the bolt grade shown on the detail match the project's standard bolt grade?"

She tests the checklist on a real submittal that week and it catches a genuine issue: a weld size on the detail that doesn't match the calc, likely missed on a first fast pass otherwise. She saves it as v1.0 in her firm's shared drive, dated, flagged as a review aid requiring independent code verification. Building and testing it took about 40 minutes, and it's now the team's shared starting point.

eng-i2-research-standards-and-precedents.walkthrough:
Ben is a civil engineer working on a low-rise commercial building in a county he hasn't worked in before, and he needs to confirm how wind exposure category is determined for the site before finalizing his structural loading assumptions. Rather than digging through PDFs blind, he opens Gemini and starts a Deep Research session instead of a normal chat.

He writes a specific, narrow research question following the lesson's format: "What does ASCE 7 require for wind exposure category determination for a low-rise building in open terrain?" He states his jurisdiction as the specific county the project is in, and for the code edition, since he's not fully sure which ASCE 7 edition the county has adopted, he writes "UNKNOWN - PLEASE HELP IDENTIFY." Gemini shows a short research plan before running; he confirms it and lets it proceed.

About twelve minutes later, the report comes back citing the relevant ASCE 7 section defining Exposure Categories B, C, and D, quoting the specific criteria for each category, and noting the publication edition, ASCE 7-22. Importantly, it flags: "This jurisdiction's adopted building code may reference an earlier edition of ASCE 7 (e.g., ASCE 7-16 via the 2021 IBC) - confirm the adopted edition with the local building department before use."

Ben sends a follow-up in the same session asking Gemini to search specifically for the most recent adopted-code reference for this county and say plainly whether it can confirm the current edition. Gemini finds a county building department page referencing the 2021 IBC, but is honest it cannot fully confirm whether a local amendment overrides the referenced ASCE 7 edition, and recommends direct confirmation.

Ben opens the actual ASCE 7-22 section himself and confirms the quoted exposure category language matches exactly, then calls the county building department and confirms they've adopted the 2021 IBC with no local amendment affecting this section. He logs the question, answer, sources checked, and date in his research notes. The process took about 30 minutes plus a five-minute call - faster than manual searching, but he never used the AI's answer directly without that final confirmation.

eng-i3-meeting-minutes-rfi-change-order-.walkthrough:
Carla is a project engineer coordinating a mid-rise building project. During a site walk, she noticed a real discrepancy: a structural detail shows a beam bearing on a 12-inch wall, but the architectural plan for the same location shows an 8-inch wall. Steel fabrication is scheduled to start in two weeks, so this needs to go out as a formal RFI fast, and it needs to be worded carefully since these documents can resurface later if there's ever a dispute.

She opens Claude and selects RFI as the document type. She pastes her notes: "Detail 5/S-301 shows beam bearing on wall but wall thickness on plan A-102 doesn't match - plan shows 8in, detail assumes 12in wall. Need clarification before fabrication, steel order due in 2 weeks."

Claude returns a structured RFI: a reference number placeholder and date, a question asking for clarification of the wall thickness at the beam bearing condition in Detail 5/S-301, a reference noting the detail assumes 12 in while Plan A-102 shows 8 in at the same location, a reason citing the fabrication deadline, and a requested response date reflecting the two-week timeline. It doesn't say which drawing is wrong or imply anyone made an error - it states the discrepancy as a fact requiring clarification.

Carla reads it carefully, since she knows RFIs can get pulled into disputes later. She asks Claude to flag any language that could be read as assigning fault, even implicitly. Claude confirms the draft is neutral and finds nothing to flag, but Carla reads it once more herself before trusting that.

She fills in the actual RFI number from her firm's numbering log and the specific dates, then routes it through her firm's standard RFI distribution process rather than sending it straight from the draft. The whole process took about 10 minutes, and the RFI reads as precise and neutral - exactly what she needs if this discrepancy is ever referenced again months later.

eng-a1-reusable-documentation-templates-.walkthrough:
Raj leads a team of six structural engineers and has noticed an inconsistency problem: when he reviews inspection reports, some engineers carefully flag every judgment call, and others - usually rushing near a deadline - write conclusions directly into the report, skipping the placeholder discipline the firm expects. He decides to build a shared template instead of relying on everyone remembering the practice on their own.

He opens Claude and works through the lesson's meta-prompt. Task type: geotechnical field observation report. Who will use it: field engineers, including newer EITs. Output needed: structured report draft with placeholders for recommendations. He includes the five fixed guardrails from the lesson exactly as given - grounding to supplied notes only, judgment placeholders, code-verification flags, a DRAFT label, and exact numeric preservation.

Claude designs a template with a guardrails preamble stating all five rules, placeholders for [PROJECT], [SITE VISIT DATE], and [SOURCE FIELD NOTES], an output structure organizing observations by test location with a recommendations placeholder, and a usage note: "v1.0 - for routine field observation write-ups only. Not for final geotechnical reports, which require full engineer analysis."

Raj wants to be sure this holds up on real, messy data before rolling it out, so he sends a genuinely messy set of past field notes and asks Claude to report where a guardrail might get bypassed. Claude flags that one ambiguous note about soil moisture could get interpreted as a bearing-capacity judgment call if the flagging instruction isn't emphasized enough, and suggests strengthening that line. Raj applies the fix.

He tests the revised template on two more past site visits, confirms the judgment placeholder consistently appears where expected, and saves it as v1.0 in the firm's shared template folder with a changelog note about why the guardrail was strengthened. He sets a six-month review reminder. Building and testing the template took about an hour spread across two sessions, but it now gives every engineer on his team - not just the careful ones - the same built-in safety net.

arc-b2-concept-narratives-that-sell-a-de.walkthrough:
Devon is an architect preparing a client presentation for a hillside residential addition. The design has real logic behind it, but his past narratives have tended to read as flat lists of features rather than a compelling story, and he wants this one to actually land with the client.

Claude returns a narrative opening with the site's grade change, explaining the split-level response as working with the slope rather than against it, tying the south orientation to daylight and the preserved oak trees, and closing on the standing-seam metal as answering two goals at once. He reads it against his drawings and it holds up factually, but one section uses the word "timeless" to describe the material choice without tying it to anything specific - it reads as filler. arc-i1-visual-concept-exploration-with-a.walkthrough:
Naomi is an architect starting concept design for a two-story home on a wooded, gently sloped lot. The client mentioned wanting a simple gabled form but is worried about the house feeling too bulky from the street, and Naomi wants to explore massing options quickly before committing time to a full 3D model. She picks Gemini's Nano Banana for this round, expecting to want several fast, conversational rounds of tweaking.

She opens Gemini and fills in the lesson's prompt. Number of images: 5. Focus: massing/form, kept as the only focus. Project context: two-story single-family home, wooded gently sloped lot, temperate climate. Design direction: exploring how a simple gabled form could break into two offset volumes to preserve views through the site and reduce apparent bulk from the street. Style notes: regional vernacular barns with simple gabled forms.

Nano Banana generates five distinct massing studies, each showing a different relationship between the two offset volumes - varying roof pitch, offset distance, and how the connector is handled. Naomi reviews them with her team; two options stand out as worth developing further, while three clearly don't solve the bulk problem.

She sends a follow-up asking for three more variations within the most promising direction, wanting more range before committing to a model. The new batch clarifies which offset distance reads best.

Before showing anything to the client, she asks for a short, natural label to put under each image - she gets back "Illustrative concept study - not a rendering or final design" - and adds it to every slide in her presentation deck. In the client meeting, she says the same thing out loud, making clear these are exploratory and not to scale.

After the client reacts positively, Naomi develops the selected direction into an actual scaled massing model and checks it against the real site survey and setback requirements - something the AI images had no way to verify. The exploration itself took about 20 minutes, giving the team a fast starting point that would otherwise have required hours of manual sketching.

arc-i2-client-facing-project-documentati.walkthrough:
Priya is an architect managing a residential project where two things are happening at once: the permit review is running two weeks behind because city comments came back late, and the client needs to make a kitchen appliance decision by the end of the month or their order gets delayed too. She needs to communicate both clearly without either burying the decision or making the delay sound worse or better than it actually is.

She opens ChatGPT and works through the lesson's prompt. Purpose: delay notice plus decision request. What's completed: site survey, with no issues found. What's in progress: revising drawings after late city comments, resubmitting in five business days. Decision needed: the appliance package selection by end of month. Next steps: resubmit permit drawings by a specific date, awaiting the appliance decision by another specific date.

ChatGPT returns a draft labeled "DRAFT - review before sending," with clear headers: Completed notes the survey is done with no issues; In Progress explains the permit delay and resubmission plan, followed by "[ARCHITECT TO ADD FRAMING: note on what this means for overall schedule]"; Decision Needed states the appliance deadline; Next Steps lists both dates.

Priya appreciates that the draft didn't guess how worried the client should be - that's a judgment call she needs to make herself. She knows this client responds better to a direct, no-cushioning tone, so she sends a follow-up describing that preference. The revised version drops the softer transitional language and gets to the point faster.

She personally writes the framing for the schedule implication - being honest that the overall completion date will likely shift by about two weeks, not glossing over it - and fills that into the placeholder herself. She reads the whole update once more, confirms the decision-needed section is impossible to miss, and sends it. Total time: about 12 minutes, and the client responded within a day with their appliance decision, avoiding a second delay stacking on top of the first.

arc-i3-planning-and-consent-document-dra.walkthrough:
Sam is an architect preparing a variance narrative for a client's rear addition. The lot has an irregular, pie-shaped geometry that pushes the proposed rear setback down to about 18 feet, and Sam believes the standard requirement in this R-2 district is 25 feet, though he hasn't independently confirmed that figure against the current ordinance yet.

He opens Claude and fills in the lesson's prompt. Submission type: variance narrative. Jurisdiction: the specific city. Project facts: the address, zoned R-2, proposing a rear addition reducing the rear setback from a believed 25ft requirement to 18ft due to the irregular lot shape, with the existing structure already non-conforming on one side setback. For known applicable sections, he honestly writes "UNKNOWN - FLAG FOR RESEARCH."

Claude returns a draft with a project description of the 400 sf addition, a zoning context section noting R-2 zoning with a [VERIFY AGAINST CURRENT ORDINANCE: confirm current rear setback, stated here as 25 ft] tag, a factual description of the resulting 18 ft setback, and a variance justification arguing the lot's non-standard shape - not a choice to maximize buildable area - is the source of the reduction, with another flag asking him to confirm the specific variance criteria required.

Sam does a careful pass checking that every regulatory claim has a flag - he asks Claude to confirm nothing slipped through unflagged, and it catches one unflagged line referencing "typical setback variance criteria," which it then flags.

He pulls the actual zoning ordinance himself, confirms the R-2 rear setback is indeed 25 ft with no recent amendment, and finds the variance criteria section, which requires demonstrating the hardship isn't self-created. He gives Claude these confirmed facts and asks it to update the draft, leaving still-unconfirmed items flagged. He routes the final draft through his firm's standard review before submission. Total time: about 40 minutes drafting, plus 20 minutes independently verifying the ordinance - non-negotiable regardless of how confident the draft sounds.
